threads.thread_goal: Align on current-state findings and prioritize main bottlenecks to tackle first.

messages.text:
Kicking off the current-state review for our Lean Production and Supply Optimization for Cleaning Products Line project_title.
I have uploaded a draft of the Current-State Production and Supply Diagnostic based on T1 into A1. It covers end-to-end flow for the main SKUs, with cycle times, changeovers, WIP levels, and a first pass at baseline KPIs that would feed into A6 and T6.
Headline bottlenecks I am seeing so far:
- Long changeovers on the multi-purpose cleaner line
- Frequent micro-stops on the filling station for disinfectants
- High WIP before final packing, driven by uneven batch sizes
Before we lock anything, I would like your reactions on:
1) Are these the right candidates for our top 3 bottlenecks for phase 1?
2) Any concerns with the baseline data sources I used for A6 (MES logs, manual time studies, and last 8 weeks of OTIF reports)?
Please add comments here so we can converge on D1 and D2.

Thanks for pulling A1 together.
On the bottlenecks, the long changeovers on the multi-purpose line definitely resonate from what I see on the floor. For the micro-stops on disinfectant filling, do we know how much of that is due to nozzle cleaning versus labeler issues? That might affect whether we treat it as one bottleneck or split root causes.
On WIP before packing, I agree it is a problem, but I am wondering if it is more a symptom of the schedule pattern than a standalone bottleneck.
For A6, using MES logs and OTIF reports makes sense. For manual time studies, did we run them across all shifts or just day shift? That could skew D2 if we are not careful.

Adding a quick note from yesterday's walk-through.
On the multi-purpose line, operators mentioned that cleaning validation steps are taking longer since the last safety update. That might be inflating the changeover time in A1, but we cannot just cut that without checking with the health and safety officer.
For the WIP before packing, I pulled a quick snapshot from last week. We had pallets sitting for up to 6 hours before final packing on two SKUs. That suggests we should keep it in the discussion for D1, even if it is schedule-driven.
On data for A6, I would be more comfortable if we cross-check OTIF with the warehouse dispatch logs, just to make sure we are not missing partial shipments.

I went through part of A1 this morning.
One thing I am not fully clear on: for the disinfectant filling micro-stops, are we counting every short pause, or only those above a certain duration? It would help me if we could have a simple summary table in A1 with counts and total downtime per cause.
Also, for the baseline KPIs in A6, do we already have OEE calculated per line, or is that still to be done under T6? I only saw OTIF and some throughput numbers in the draft.

From a project steering angle, I want to make sure the bottlenecks we pick for D1 are the ones that most affect customer delivery and cost.
Looking at the early A6 view, the multi-purpose line has the highest volume and the most frequent rush orders. So long changeovers there seem like a must-have in the top 3.
Can we quantify, even roughly, how much OTIF loss is linked to the disinfectant filling micro-stops versus the WIP before packing? That will help us justify the focus when we present the diagnostic to the chief executive officer and sales manager.

From the purchasing side, one angle I would like to add is raw material availability.
In A1, there is a note that some of the WIP before packing is caused by waiting for caps and labels. That links to T4 and T11 later, but it also means that if we treat WIP before packing as a bottleneck for D1, we should be clear how much is internal versus supplier-driven.
For A6, I can help validate the material cost per unit baseline once we have the final list of KPIs under T6. Right now I only see a rough average, not split by product family.

On the disinfectant filling micro-stops: in A1 I grouped them into three main buckets so far – nozzle cleaning, labeler jams, and short pauses for manual inspections. Nozzle cleaning is about 45 percent of the downtime, labeler 35 percent, inspections 20 percent. I can add the summary table you suggested so it is clearer.
For WIP before packing, I agree it is partly a symptom of the schedule. However, given the 6-hour waits that 538904 mentioned, I think it is still worth treating as a bottleneck candidate, at least until we see the impact of the new schedule from T2.
On the manual time studies, they were done on day and evening shifts, but not night shift. I will flag that gap in A1 and A6 so we do not overstate precision for D2.

Good catch on OEE.
Right now, A6 only has OTIF, average lead time, and basic throughput per line. OEE by line is still to be completed under T6. I propose we:
- Use the current OTIF and lead time as provisional baselines for D2
- Add OEE by line as a follow-up once we finish the data pull with operations and finance
I will also add the downtime table you requested into A1 so we have counts and total minutes per cause.

I did a quick check on last month's OTIF incidents.
- About 60 percent of late orders on multi-purpose cleaner link back to long changeovers and sequence changes.
- For disinfectants, roughly 25 percent of late orders mention filling line issues, which lines up with the micro-stops.
- The WIP before packing shows up more as extended lead time than outright misses, but it still affects how much buffer we need.
Based on that, my suggestion for D1 would be:
1) Long changeovers on the multi-purpose line
2) Disinfectant filling micro-stops
3) WIP before packing on key SKUs
Open to challenge if anyone sees a better third candidate.

I support that list for D1.
On the third point, maybe we can narrow WIP before packing to the top 3 SKUs where it hurts the most, so we do not spread ourselves too thin in phase 1.
If we agree, we can reflect that scope clearly in A1 and in the roadmap later in A5.

From my side, that top 3 works.
For the WIP before packing, I will check which of those top SKUs are most exposed to supplier delays so we can connect this with T4 and T11. That way, when we present A1 and A6, we can already show how supplier actions will support the bottleneck work.

I am comfortable locking those three bottlenecks for phase 1, with the refinement that WIP before packing focuses on the top 3 SKUs.
So for D1, we are agreeing on:
1) Long changeovers on the multi-purpose cleaner line
2) Disinfectant filling micro-stops (nozzle cleaning and labeler)
3) Excess WIP before packing on the top 3 SKUs
On D2, I would like a clear statement of which KPIs and data sources we treat as baseline in A6, even if some are marked as provisional. Can you summarize that, 181683, so we can close D2 as well?

Just to double-check before we close D2: for OTIF, are we using the last 8 weeks only, or a longer period? I am asking because we had that one-off disruption six weeks ago that might distort the baseline.
If we keep 8 weeks, maybe we should at least note that event in A6 so it is not misread later.

Here is a proposed summary for D2 and the A6 baseline:
KPIs:
- OTIF by product family
- Average lead time from order to shipment
- Throughput per line (units per hour)
- Provisional OEE per line (to be completed under T6)
Data sources:
- Last 8 weeks of OTIF reports from sales and logistics
- MES logs for cycle times and downtime
- Manual time studies on day and evening shifts
- Warehouse dispatch logs to cross-check shipments
I agree with 261854 that we should annotate the one-off disruption in A6 so it is clear. We can still use the 8-week window but mark that week as exceptional.
If there are no objections, I suggest we treat this as our agreed baseline for D2.

Works for me.
Let us record D2 as agreed with that KPI list and data sources, plus the note on the exceptional week in A6.
Next step will be to use this baseline as the reference when we evaluate the impact of the new schedule from T2 and the roadmap in A5.

To close the loop on TH1:
- I will update A1 with the finalized top 3 bottlenecks from D1, including the narrowed scope on WIP before packing.
- I will refresh A6 with the agreed KPI list and data sources from D2, and annotate the exceptional week.
Once that is done, we can move into T2 design work using these as our reference.

threads.thread_goal: Lock the new production schedule design and related SOP changes.

messages.text:
Following the diagnostic in A1 and the baselines in A6, I have drafted an optimized weekly production schedule in A2 as part of T2, plus an outline of the SOP changes we would need under T3.
Key elements of the proposed schedule:
- Fixed sequence on the multi-purpose line to minimize changeovers, with two planned campaign blocks per week
- Smoother loading of the disinfectant filling line to reduce micro-stops, including short planned pauses for nozzle cleaning
- Smaller, more frequent batches for the top 3 SKUs that were driving WIP before packing
On SOPs (future A3), the main changes would be:
- Standardized changeover checklist and timing targets
- Defined cleaning and inspection windows on the filling line
- Clear handover rules between production and packing to avoid WIP build-up
I would like feedback before we move to D3 and D4.
Questions:
1) Does the schedule in A2 cover demand for the last 8 weeks without stockouts when you simulate it?
2) Are there any safety or regulatory concerns with the proposed SOP scope, especially around cleaning and PPE, that we should capture in A7 and T12?

I ran a quick check on A2 using the last 4 weeks of demand.
The fixed sequence on the multi-purpose line seems to work, but we are tight on one SKU when there is a spike in week 3. We still meet demand, but only with minimal buffer.
On the disinfectant line, the planned cleaning windows help stabilize throughput in the simulation.
For SOPs in A3, I like the idea of a standardized changeover checklist. We should make sure the health and safety officer reviews any changes to cleaning agents or PPE via A7 and T12 before we roll them out.

I focused on the WIP before packing.
With the smaller, more frequent batches in A2, the simulation shows average waiting time before packing dropping from around 5 hours to about 2 hours for the top 3 SKUs.
One concern: the packing team mentioned that too many small batches could increase their changeover frequency. We might need an SOP in A3 that defines a minimum batch size for packing, or a rule for grouping similar SKUs.
On safety, the proposed cleaning windows should be checked against the latest cleaning industry health and safety measures. We should capture that in A7 and make sure T12 includes verification of ventilation and chemical handling steps.

I tried to test A2 against the full 8 weeks, but I am not sure I set the parameters correctly.
In the sheet, for the multi-purpose line, do we assume any overtime, or is it strictly within current shift patterns? When I left overtime at zero, I saw a small backlog building in week 6.
Also, for the SOP outline in A3, could we add a simple section on how operators should escalate when they see repeated micro-stops outside the planned cleaning windows? That might help us capture issues in A8 later during the pilot.

From a governance point of view, I want to be sure that the schedule we approve for D3 does not require extra headcount and does not jeopardize confirmed delivery dates.
Can we confirm that the A2 template:
- Stays within existing shift patterns, with overtime only as an exception
- Meets all confirmed customer orders in the 8-week backtest
On SOP scope for D4, I would like us to be explicit about which process steps are changing versus which remain as-is. That will help with the communication plan in A5 and with training under T3.

On A2 parameters: the base case assumes current shift patterns with no structural overtime. There is a separate field where you can add exceptional overtime for specific weeks. For the 8-week test, I used zero overtime and still met demand, but with low buffer in weeks 3 and 6.
I will add a note in A2 explaining that, and we can decide if we want to allow a small amount of planned overtime in peak weeks or adjust the sequence slightly.
On the SOP outline in A3, I like the idea of an escalation section. We can link that to the issue log in A8 during the pilot so that repeated micro-stops trigger a standard response.

To your points:
- With the current A2 setup, we stay within existing shifts. The only risk is the low buffer in a couple of weeks, which we can manage with a small safety stock adjustment under T8 rather than changing headcount.
- In the 8-week backtest I ran, we did not miss any confirmed orders, but we had two cases where we shipped very close to the promised date.
For SOP scope in A3, I suggest we mark the following as changed steps:
1) Changeover sequence and checks on the multi-purpose line
2) Planned cleaning and inspection windows on the disinfectant line
3) Handover rules between production and packing for the top 3 SKUs
Everything else would be explicitly listed as unchanged, but still referenced in A3 for completeness.

On the packing side, I spoke briefly with the warehouse manager.
They are comfortable with more frequent batches as long as we define a minimum batch size and avoid mixing too many label variants in a single shift. We can capture that in the packing SOP section of A3.
For safety, they also asked that A7 and T12 explicitly check pallet stability and stacking rules when we change batch sizes, since that can affect how pallets are wrapped and stored.

Given the feedback, here is a proposal for D3:
- Approve the A2 weekly schedule template with current shift patterns and no structural overtime
- Allow for exceptional overtime only in peak weeks, to be pre-approved and documented
- Confirm that the 8-week backtest meets all confirmed orders, with low but acceptable buffer in weeks 3 and 6
On D4 and SOP scope in A3, I propose we formally include as changed steps:
1) Multi-purpose line changeover sequence and checklist
2) Disinfectant filling cleaning and inspection windows
3) Handover rules and minimum batch sizes between production and packing for the top 3 SKUs
All other steps remain unchanged but will be referenced for context.
If there are no strong objections, I suggest we record D3 and D4 on that basis.

I am aligned with that proposal.
Let us record D3 as approval of the A2 schedule template under current shifts, with exceptional overtime only in peak weeks, and confirmation that the 8-week backtest meets demand.
For D4, we sign off on the SOP change scope you listed for A3, with the condition that the health and safety officer validates all changes via A7 and T12 before go-live.
This gives us a clear basis for T3 and for the pilot design in T9.

Thanks for clarifying.
I will update my local copy of A2 with the correct parameters and note the exceptional overtime rule.
For A3, once the health and safety officer has reviewed the draft via A7 and T12, it would be helpful to have a short training checklist so line leads know exactly which points to cover with operators under T3.

To wrap up TH2:
- I will finalize A2 with the agreed schedule template and document the rules on exceptional overtime.
- I will update the A3 SOP outline to reflect the approved scope from D4 and route it to the health and safety officer using A7 and T12.
- Once we have sign-off, we can start drafting detailed SOPs and plan operator training under T3, feeding into the pilot in T9.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on supplier segmentation and negotiation priorities.

messages.text:
I have uploaded a first draft of the Supplier Segmentation and Performance Matrix into A4, based on T4.
The draft segments key raw material suppliers (surfactants, solvents, fragrances, caps, labels, bottles) by cost, quality, lead time, and risk.
Initial segmentation proposal in A4:
- Strategic: top surfactant and bottle suppliers
- Preferred: main fragrance and label suppliers
- Backup: secondary caps and some smaller packaging suppliers
Before we move to D5 and D6, I would like your input on:
1) Are the scoring thresholds in A4 reasonable for classifying suppliers as strategic, preferred, or backup?
2) Which 5 suppliers should we prioritize for renegotiation under T5, considering the bottlenecks we identified in A1 and the schedule in A2?

Thanks for pulling A4 together.
From the production side, the most sensitive materials for our bottlenecks are:
- Caps and labels for the top 3 SKUs that were driving WIP before packing in A1
- Bottles for the multi-purpose line
- Certain disinfectant components that have long lead times
Looking at A4, I wonder if some of the cap and label suppliers should be moved up from backup to preferred, given their impact on the new schedule in A2.
On thresholds, the current cut-off for lead time risk seems a bit high. A supplier with 4-week lead time and frequent delays might still be classified as preferred. Maybe we should tighten that before we lock D5.

I agree with 181683 on the caps and labels.
In the last month, we had two cases where label deliveries contributed to WIP before packing. Those suppliers are currently marked as backup in A4, but operationally they are more critical.
For D6 and T5, my suggestion for top negotiation targets would be:
1) Main bottle supplier for the multi-purpose line
2) Primary cap supplier for the top 3 SKUs
3) Primary label supplier for the top 3 SKUs
4) Main disinfectant component supplier with long lead time
5) One backup packaging supplier we want to qualify as a more reliable alternative
We should also make sure T11 includes monitoring for these specific suppliers.

From a business case angle, I want to balance risk and savings.
In A4, some of the strategic suppliers have very strong quality and reliability but higher prices. For D5, I do not want us to push them too hard on price if it risks service.
Could we adjust the segmentation thresholds so that:
- Strategic suppliers must meet a minimum reliability score, even if cost is not the lowest
- Backup suppliers are clearly those with either higher risk or lower strategic importance
Once that is clear, we can pick the top 5 for T5 in a way that supports both the schedule in A2 and the budget work in T10.

Good points.
I can tighten the lead time risk threshold in A4 so that suppliers with more than 3 weeks lead time and frequent delays are flagged as higher risk.
For the caps and labels, I will re-score those suppliers based on their impact on the top 3 SKUs and likely move at least one of them from backup to preferred.
On the strategic versus preferred distinction, I will also add a minimum reliability score for strategic suppliers, as 472928 suggested.
Once I update A4, I will share a short summary here so we can close D5.

Looking at A4 from the shop floor perspective, one thing I notice is that some smaller local suppliers are marked as backup, but they have been very responsive when we had urgent needs.
Is there a way in A4 to capture responsiveness separately from standard lead time? That might help us decide who to include in the top 5 for T5, especially for caps and labels.

That is a fair point.
I can add a responsiveness sub-score in A4, based on how quickly suppliers react to rush orders or issues. It will not change the main segmentation alone, but it can help us choose negotiation priorities under T5.
I will also make sure T11 includes responsiveness as one of the risk indicators we monitor over time.

Once you update A4 with the tighter lead time thresholds and the reliability requirement for strategic suppliers, I think we can formalize D5 as:
- Strategic: high reliability, acceptable cost, and critical to the multi-purpose or disinfectant lines
- Preferred: good performance but less critical, or with some manageable risk
- Backup: used mainly for contingency or non-critical items
This will give us a clear basis for T11 and for the negotiation focus in T5.

I support that framing for D5.
Let us record D5 as approval of the segmentation categories and thresholds in A4, with the updated lead time and reliability criteria.
For D6, I agree with the list 538904 proposed earlier, but I would like 405215 to confirm that these 5 suppliers also offer meaningful negotiation levers for T5 without putting supply at risk.

On the 5 suppliers suggested by 538904:
1) Main bottle supplier: we have room to discuss minimum order quantities and delivery frequency, which would help align with A2.
2) Primary cap supplier: there is some flexibility on safety stock at their site and on lead time.
3) Primary label supplier: we can negotiate better prioritization for the top 3 SKUs.
4) Main disinfectant component supplier: less room on price, but we can work on lead time and allocation.
5) Backup packaging supplier: we can formalize them as a more robust alternative with clearer service levels.
I am comfortable treating these as our top 5 for T5 under D6, as long as we approach the strategic ones with a focus on reliability and flexibility rather than just price.

That works for production.
If we can secure more flexible deliveries from the bottle, cap, and label suppliers, it will make it much easier to keep the A2 schedule stable and avoid WIP before packing.
For T11, it would be good if we set clear escalation steps when any of these 5 suppliers hit risk thresholds, so we can react before it affects OTIF in A6.

To close TH3:
- We have agreed D5: the segmentation categories and thresholds in A4, with tightened lead time and reliability criteria.
- We have agreed D6: the top 5 suppliers to prioritize for T5 negotiations, focusing on bottles, caps, labels, a key disinfectant component, and one backup packaging supplier.
Next, 405215 will move ahead with T5 discussions and finalize T11 with risk indicators and escalation steps, especially for these 5 suppliers.

threads.thread_goal: Finalize implementation roadmap, pilot scope, and risk mitigations.

messages.text:
I have posted a draft of the Implementation Roadmap and Communication Plan in A5, covering T7 and linking to T8, T9, and T10.
The proposal is to run a pilot on the multi-purpose cleaner family first, using the new schedule from A2 and the SOP changes from A3.
Draft pilot parameters in A5:
- Duration: 3 weeks
- Scope: multi-purpose cleaner SKUs, including the top 3 that drive WIP before packing
- Success criteria: no missed customer deliveries, at least 10 percent reduction in changeover time, and reduced WIP before packing versus the A6 baseline
Before we lock D7 and D8, I would like your feedback on:
1) Is the pilot scope and duration appropriate, or should we adjust?
2) Are the success criteria clear and measurable enough for T9 and for the updated business case in T10?
3) Any risks or dependencies we have not captured in A5, especially around warehouse alignment in T8 and supplier readiness from T5 and T11?

On the pilot scope in A5, starting with the multi-purpose cleaner family makes sense, since that is where we have the biggest changeover gains.
I am slightly concerned that 3 weeks might be short to see stable behavior, especially if we hit any unplanned downtime. Maybe we could plan for 4 weeks but define a minimum of 3 weeks of good data.
The success criteria look measurable. I would add one more: no increase in safety incidents or near-misses, using the checklist in A7 as part of T9.
For T8, we need to make sure the warehouse has updated reorder points and safety stock for the pilot SKUs before we start, otherwise we might confuse schedule effects with inventory issues.

From the line perspective, a 4-week window would give us at least one full cycle of demand patterns for the multi-purpose family.
On risks, I would highlight:
- Operator learning curve on the new SOPs in A3
- Potential delays if suppliers do not align with the new delivery patterns from T5
We should use A8 during the pilot to log any issues daily under T9, including near-misses and schedule deviations, so we can adjust quickly.

On supplier readiness, for the pilot period I can coordinate with the main bottle, cap, and label suppliers we selected under D6 and T5.
We should reflect in A5 that, before the pilot starts, we will:
- Confirm delivery schedules for pilot SKUs
- Set temporary safety stock levels at suppliers where possible
Also, for T11, I will set up a simple weekly check on risk indicators for these suppliers during the pilot, so we can react quickly if something drifts.

I have a question on the success criteria.
For the 10 percent reduction in changeover time, are we comparing against the average from A6, or a more recent period? And will we measure it per changeover or as an average over the pilot weeks?
It would help me if A5 could include a simple table showing the baseline values and the target values for each KPI, so line leads can see what we are aiming for.

I like the suggestion to extend the pilot window.
How about we define D7 as:
- Pilot product family: multi-purpose cleaners, including the top 3 SKUs
- Duration: 4 weeks, with at least 3 weeks of usable data
- Success criteria: no missed deliveries, at least 10 percent reduction in average changeover time versus the A6 baseline, reduced WIP before packing, and no increase in safety incidents as per A7
On D8, I want to make sure A5 clearly shows the phases beyond the pilot, including when we would extend to disinfectants and how T8 and T10 fit in.
If we can align on that, we can finalize A5 under T7.

For the 10 percent changeover reduction, I propose we use the average changeover time from A6 for the multi-purpose line as the baseline, and measure the average across all changeovers during the pilot.
I will add a table in A5 that lists, for each KPI:
- Baseline value from A6
- Target value for the pilot
- Data source and owner
That should make it easier for line leads and for the T9 team to track progress.

I am comfortable with the D7 parameters you outlined.
On the roadmap in A5, I suggest we explicitly include a short stabilization phase after the pilot, before we roll the new schedule to other product families. That will give us time to digest the A8 issue log and adjust SOPs in A3 if needed.
For T8, we should also plan a small trial run in the warehouse for one of the pilot SKUs before the full pilot starts, to validate the new reorder points and safety stock.

From purchasing, I am aligned with D7.
I will make sure the suppliers identified in TH3 are ready for the 4-week pilot window and that any temporary arrangements are reflected in the cost assumptions for T10.
For A5, it might be useful to add a simple communication line for suppliers, so they know when the pilot starts and what changes they might see in order patterns.

Based on the feedback, I propose we finalize D8 as follows:
- Approve the overall implementation roadmap in A5, with phases: preparation, 4-week pilot on multi-purpose cleaners, stabilization, and subsequent rollout to other families
- Confirm that T7 covers risk and dependency mapping, including warehouse alignment under T8 and supplier readiness under T5 and T11
- Approve the communication plan in A5 for internal teams and key suppliers
This will give us a clear path to update the business case in T10 once we have pilot results.

I am aligned with D8 as you summarized.
Next concrete steps from operations:
- Finalize the pilot plan in A5 under T7, including the KPI table and the safety criterion using A7
- Coordinate with the warehouse manager to complete T8 for at least one pilot SKU before the pilot start
- Prepare the T9 pilot execution plan, including daily updates to A8 and a short standup routine for the pilot team.

To close TH4:
- D7 is confirmed: pilot on the multi-purpose cleaner family for 4 weeks, with clear success criteria versus A6 and safety checks via A7.
- D8 is confirmed: approval of the implementation roadmap and communication plan in A5, covering preparation, pilot, stabilization, and rollout.
Once we have pilot results logged in A8, we will update the business case under T10 and share it with the broader stakeholder group.
